newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Firm oil prices seen helping Indonesian economy.
newsitem.headline: Firm oil prices seen helping Indonesian economy.

text.p: Indonesian Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita said on Thursday a recent rally in oil prices would help the country's economy but predicted the rally would end within a year.
"In the short term, certainly the country will receive more revenue from oil exports. Certainly it will help reduce the current-account deficit," Ginanjar told reporters.
"We will use the money to accelerate the repayment of our commercial loans and to settle priority development projects," he said.
"However, we have experienced in the past that if oil prices are too high, people will produce more oil which will then depress prices," Ginanjar said.
"So we should not expect strong oil prices to last too long. From our experience it will not last even for one year," he said.
The minister said he did not want Indonesia's economy to be too dependent on oil-export revenues and thus be vulnerable to price fluctuations.

State oil company Pertamina has said Indonesia will get around $600 million for every increase of one dollar in the price of crude above the price envisaged in the state budget. However, 47 percent of that amount will go towards purchasing crude to feed its refineries, it has said.
Indonesia had set a price of $16.50 per barrel of oil in its 1996/97 (April-March) budget.

The country had estimated its current-account deficit would widen to $8.7 billion in fiscal 1996/97, or about four percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The deficit was $7 billion, or about 3.2 percent of GDP, in 1995/96.
Indonesia, a member of OPEC, produces around 1.60 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and condensate. About 760,000 bpd of that are exported.
London November futures for international benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude on Wednesday hovered around the $25 level it broke earlier this week for the first time since the Gulf War.
